originalGroup.material:
A dictionary of my own examples

My English teacher ____1____ (suggest) keeping a vocabulary notebook at the beginning of last term. I first copied long lists of words, but soon discovered that a neat list was not the same ____2____ knowing how to use them.

Now I choose fewer words and write a short example for each one. The example should be something ____3____ I can understand without searching another page. If I borrow a sentence from a book, I note where it came from instead of pretending it is mine.

I also try ____4____ (add) a phrase rather than an isolated word when the combination matters. A verb may take a particular preposition, and that small detail can be difficult ____5____ (remember) later.

Once a week, I look back without ____6____ (cover) the examples at first. Then I hide the new words and see whether I can supply them. If I cannot, I change the example or look for another one rather than copying the same list again.

The notebook has become ____7____ (useful) than my original collection because it helps me ask specific questions. Some entries include two ____8____ (meaning) of a word, with different situations beside them.

I do not expect to remember everything immediately. The point is to make the next encounter easier. When I meet a familiar expression, I check whether ____9____ (I) example still makes sense. Learning a word is part of learning ____10____ it works, not merely recognising its shape.

originalGroup.material:
Bubbles in bread dough

Our school cook showed us a small piece of bread dough. It looked different from a mixture of flour and water because it contained yeast. She explained that yeast consists of tiny living ____1____ (organism) that can produce gas as they use sugar.

The gas becomes trapped in the dough, helping it rise. That does not mean every mixture grows at the same speed. Temperature, ingredients and time all matter. The cook asked us ____2____ (notice) the conditions rather than remember a single number as a rule for every recipe.

We looked at two covered bowls ____3____ had been prepared earlier. One dough had risen ____4____ (high) than the other. We were not allowed to decide that yeast alone explained the difference without knowing how each bowl had been prepared.

After ____5____ (observe) the dough, we watched the cook shape it. She handled it confidently, but paused to explain what she was feeling. A written instruction could give useful guidance, yet experience helped her respond ____6____ changes in the mixture.

The finished bread ____7____ (bake) by the kitchen staff. We did not work with the ovens ourselves. Later, we compared a cut slice with the raw dough, noticing the spaces inside.

The visit gave us ____8____ (we) first close look at a familiar food's preparation. I wrote a short ____9____ (describe) for the school newsletter. It was ____10____ introduction to a process, not a claim that I could now make every kind of bread.
